frontier-program.title: Get started with the Microsoft Copilot Frontier Program
frontier-program.notes: The Frontier program gives organizations preview access to emerging Microsoft 365 capabilities before general availability. Opted-in IT admins can evaluate new Copilot agents and other AI and non-AI experiences, judge readiness for broader rollout and send feedback to Microsoft. It is managed per tenant, and admins choose whether all users or only selected users and groups receive Frontier features. Frontier sits beside the Standard release (features at general availability) and Deferred release (about 30 days later) options, and a user can be in Frontier and also on either of those. Admins need the AI Administrator, Security Administrator or Office Apps Administrator role. A Copilot license is not required to enroll users, but users need one to see Copilot-related Frontier features. Features can take roughly three hours to appear after switching Frontier on. The features are previews that may change or be withdrawn, may fall outside normal support commitments, are not covered by HIPAA BAA terms and do not comply with ISO 27001, 27002 or 27018. Features using third-party AI providers require explicit admin approval of each model.

fully-qualified-domain-name.title: Fully qualified domain name (Wikipedia)
fully-qualified-domain-name.notes: A fully qualified domain name, also called an absolute domain name, states a host's exact position in the Domain Name System tree, so it can be read in only one way. Labels are separated by dots and read from right to left, from the top-level domain down to the host; in somehost.example.com, com sits directly under the root, example under com, and somehost under example.com. The root itself is an empty label that is written as a trailing dot, which is required in DNS zone files and normally implied or omitted by applications. Each label may be 1 to 63 octets long and the whole name is limited to 255 octets including dots. A relative or partially qualified name leaves out some labels. Inside DNS messages names are not stored as dotted text; the dotted form appears in places such as TXT records, resolver settings, hosts files and URLs. Web addresses usually use FQDNs so they resolve the same way on any network. Protocols differ in what they accept: HTTP permits relative hostnames, while SMTP does not.

generative-engine-optimization.title: Generative engine optimization (Wikipedia)
generative-engine-optimization.notes: Generative engine optimization is the practice of structuring content and managing online presence so that a brand or website appears more often in answers produced by generative AI systems. It aims to influence how large language models retrieve, summarize and present information. The page lists related names such as answer engine optimization, LLM optimization, AI optimization and AI SEO, and says they are often used interchangeably, with no agreed definition in academic literature as of early 2026. In practice, tools monitor how brands and websites are cited or referenced in AI answers. The page reports Google guidance published in 2026 stating that optimizing for generative AI search is still SEO. It also notes an unverified claim that practitioners shifted from keyword placement towards semantic relevance, and points out that the monetization of AI search results by OpenAI and Google is related but not part of GEO. The article gives only a high-level picture and does not describe specific techniques or how effectiveness is measured.

gentle-ai.title: Gentle-AI (GitHub repository)
gentle-ai.notes: Gentle-AI is an open-source, MIT-licensed tool by Alan Buscaglia under the Gentleman Programming name that configures AI coding agents a developer already uses; it never installs an agent itself. The repository describes it as a deterministic engineering environment and lists support for around 17 to 18 agents, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, VS Code Copilot, Gemini CLI and Windsurf. It adds persistent memory through a component called Engram, a workflow called Organic-Driven Development that keeps small tasks light and gives larger approved work a recoverable feature document, rules for when subagents may be used, and a test-first default when a runnable test exists. A review step called Receipt-Driven Development freezes the candidate change before evaluation, is on by default and stays informational, leaving commit, push and release decisions with the user. A binary reads change state from disk and reports one of four states: Working, Checking, Ready or Needs your decision. Further parts include a skills library, a deny-list for sensitive files, config backups before writes and a doctor health check. The benchmark figures on the page are self-reported single runs.

git-branch.title: Branching (version control) (Wikipedia)
git-branch.notes: In version control, a branch is a copy of an object under revision control, such as a file or directory tree, that can be changed separately from the original so that the two diverge. Branches are also called trees, streams or codelines; the source of a copy is its parent or upstream, and a branch without a parent is the trunk, also known as mainline, baseline or master. Branching lets teams work on fixes, features or version integration in parallel without destabilizing the main codebase, and changes are merged back after testing. The page describes trunk-based development, feature branching, stable release branches that receive occasional fixes merged back to the trunk, and long-running branches for slow-moving work. Vendor branches hold external upstream code whose updates are merged into the main line. A copy that is never meant to be merged back is a fork. HEAD refers to the latest commit on a branch, not to the branch itself. Default main-branch names differ between tools: CVS uses MAIN, Git defaults to master, and GitHub and GitLab switched to main. Merge conflicts can arise when integrating changes.

git-commit.title: Commit (version control) (Wikipedia)
git-commit.notes: In version control, a commit sends the latest source code changes to the repository, where they become part of the head revision. Unlike a commit in data management, a version control commit is kept in the repository indefinitely. Other users who update or check out receive the newest committed version by default, but they can also retrieve an earlier one, and the system makes it easy to roll back to previous versions, so a commit remains protected even after being applied. The page illustrates the Git workflow: stage files with the add command, record them with the commit command and a message, then push to a remote such as origin on a branch such as main. A shortcut with the -a option stages and commits all modified tracked files in one step. For Mercurial it shows the equivalent sequence of add, commit with a message, and push to the default branch. The article is short and gives no historical account of the concept.

git.title: Git (Wikipedia)
git.notes: Git is a distributed version control system that tracks changes to source code or other data and is now the most widely used such system among developers. Linus Torvalds created it in April 2005 after the free licence for BitKeeper, used for Linux kernel development, was withdrawn; Junio Hamano took over maintenance in July 2005 and version 1.0 followed in December 2005. Every developer holds a full local copy of the repository with its history, so most work needs no network or central server. Branching and merging are fast because a branch is only a reference to a commit, and Git stores snapshots of directory trees rather than per-file deltas. Each commit ID depends on all prior history, in a structure similar to a Merkle tree, which guards against corruption. Objects are stored as blobs, trees, commits and tags, with delta-compressed packfiles. Repositories can be shared over HTTP(S), SSH or the Git protocol. Git itself offers no pull requests or access control; hosting services such as GitHub and GitLab supply them. Stack Overflow surveys showed Git use rising from about 69 percent in 2015 to about 94 percent in 2022.

github-copilot-cli.title: About GitHub Copilot CLI (GitHub Docs)
github-copilot-cli.notes: GitHub Copilot CLI lets people use GitHub Copilot directly from the terminal to answer questions, write and debug code and work with GitHub.com, for example asking it to change a project and open a pull request. It acts as an agent that you can steer during a session, and it is available on all Copilot plans on Linux, macOS and Windows (PowerShell or WSL); organization users need their organization to enable the CLI policy. Interactive mode, started with the copilot command, offers an ask/execute mode and a plan mode in which Copilot asks clarifying questions and builds a plan before writing code. Programmatic mode takes a single prompt through a flag, completes the task and exits. Local sandboxing can restrict file, network and system access, and a cloud sandbox is in public preview. Customization includes custom instructions, MCP servers, custom agents, hooks, skills and Copilot Memory. Because it can run commands and edit files, the page advises reviewing actions, using trusted directories and treating the allow-all-tools option as high risk; deny rules take precedence. Context is compacted automatically near 95 percent of the token limit.

github-copilot-coding-agent.title: About GitHub Copilot cloud agent (GitHub Docs)
github-copilot-coding-agent.notes: This GitHub Docs page describes Copilot's agentic, delegated-work capability, the Copilot cloud agent, which researches a repository, plans changes and implements them in the background in a cloud environment rather than in the local IDE. It edits files and runs tests and linters, and it can open a pull request for a task, review pull requests and, with a Watch and fix option, work on blockers such as failed Actions workflows or merge conflicts. Two environments are compared: a GitHub Actions-based one, limited to a single repository per run with a 59-minute maximum and 28-day data retention, and a cloud sandbox whose sessions are resumable across clients and can span several repositories in one organization. Copilot works on one branch at a time and opens one pull request per task; rulesets or branch protection can block pull request creation unless an admin allows a bypass, and only GitHub-hosted repositories are supported. Sessions started with write access can change code, otherwise they are read-only. The page stresses that output can be incorrect or suboptimal and must be reviewed and tested by people.

golden-image.title: Create a golden image in Azure Virtual Desktop
golden-image.notes: For Azure Virtual Desktop, a golden image is a custom VM image that contains all the apps and configuration settings wanted on session hosts. The page walks through creating it in the Azure portal: choose a base OS (multi-session Windows 10 or 11 or Windows Server for pooled host pools, Enterprise images for personal pools), create a base VM, take snapshots for rollback, install apps and updates, clean up, take a final snapshot and then run sysprep to generalize it. Practical rules include removing a domain-joined VM from the domain first, disabling antivirus that can make sysprep fail, avoiding the Unified Write Filter and not installing or registering the AVD agent on the image, because the registration token would expire. After shutdown the VM is captured to an Azure Compute Gallery, which Microsoft recommends for production because it supports versioning and replication, or to a simpler managed image. The source VM becomes unusable after capture, so a failed attempt should be rebuilt from the last snapshot, and images should not be built from existing custom images or from VMs already in a host pool.

google-cloud-interconnect.title: Cloud Interconnect overview (Google Cloud)
google-cloud-interconnect.notes: Cloud Interconnect provides low-latency, high-availability connections for moving data between networks without crossing the public internet, using a dedicated connection or a service provider's dedicated link. Connection types include Dedicated Interconnect (direct physical link from on-premises to Google's network), Partner Interconnect (through a supported provider), Cross-Cloud Interconnect (direct link to another cloud provider's network), Partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect, and Cross-Site Interconnect for linking on-premises sites. Types can be combined. Reliability is chosen at setup: a critical production layout targets a 99.99 percent uptime SLA, a non-critical layout 99.9 percent, and a no-SLA option exists but is discouraged for important workloads. Partner Interconnect VLAN attachments range from 50 Mbps to 50 Gbps, and 100-Gbps connections can be requested at listed locations. VPC internal IP addresses are reachable from on-premises without NAT or a VPN, provided the address ranges do not overlap. Interconnect traffic is not encrypted by default; MACsec or HA VPN over Interconnect can add encryption. Dedicated and Partner Interconnect can also help reduce egress costs.

governance-risk-compliance.title: Governance, risk management, and compliance (Wikipedia)
governance-risk-compliance.notes: Governance, risk and compliance (GRC) is an integrated approach that organizations use to meet regulatory requirements while operating effectively. It emerged in the 2000s to handle increasingly complex financial compliance and is now applied to technical, environmental and health and safety demands as well. Governance covers the processes directors set up to shape structure and assign roles; risk management anticipates and handles threats to reaching objectives under uncertainty; compliance means following legal and regulatory boundaries and voluntary ones such as internal policies. The point of combining them is to synchronize information and activities, improve reporting and reduce duplicated work compared with separate silos. The page traces the idea through COSO in the 1970s, the UK Turnbull Report in the 1990s and the Sarbanes-Oxley Act after Enron, and notes that early GRC software appeared in 2002 and the term itself was published in 2007 by OCEG founder Scott Mitchell. Frameworks it names include COSO ERM, the Three Lines Model, COBIT and ISO standards such as 31000 and 37301. Current themes are ESG reporting, board diversity disclosure, AI governance and automated cloud GRC platforms.

gpu.title: Graphics processing unit (Wikipedia)
gpu.notes: A graphics processing unit is a specialized electronic circuit for digital image processing and for accelerating computer graphics. It may sit on a discrete graphics card or be integrated into motherboards, phones, PCs, workstations and consoles. Graphics tasks are largely independent, so modern GPUs spread them over hundreds or thousands of parallel calculation units, which also suits other highly parallel problems; they often run custom programs called shaders. Performance depends on fabrication process, clock speed, caches and the number of compute blocks, and is commonly quoted in FLOPS. Discrete GPUs have dedicated video memory with high bandwidth, whereas integrated GPUs share system RAM, which is cheaper but less capable. Beyond rendering and gaming, GPUs are increasingly used for AI training and inference because they accelerate linear algebra, and for general-purpose computing such as simulation and scientific work; NVIDIA's CUDA from 2007 became the first widely adopted programming model for this. Newer GPUs add dedicated hardware for ray tracing, video encoding and AI acceleration. The page also gives a history from 1960s graphics terminals through programmable shaders to today's AI-oriented cores.

group-expiration-policy.title: Configure Microsoft 365 group expiration (Microsoft Entra)
group-expiration-policy.notes: The expiration policy manages the lifecycle of Microsoft 365 groups in Microsoft Entra ID. An organization can have one policy, and it applies only to Microsoft 365 groups. The lifetime is set in days (30 or more in the portal), and scope can be all groups, up to 500 selected groups or none. Groups with recent activity in SharePoint, Outlook, Teams or Viva Engage renew automatically, roughly 35 days before expiry. For groups that do not renew, owners receive emails 30, 15 and 1 day before expiration, and ownerless groups notify an alternate address set in the policy. Microsoft does not delete a group before the last notice has been sent. An expired group is deleted one day after its expiration date and can be restored for 30 days, a period that cannot be changed, after which Planner, Sites and Teams data are permanently removed unless retention policies or legal holds apply. When the policy is first enabled, older groups are set to 35 days until expiration. Licensing requires owning, though not assigning, Entra ID P1 or P2 for members of affected groups.

group-managed-service-accounts.title: Group Managed Service Accounts overview (Microsoft Learn)
group-managed-service-accounts.notes: A group managed service account is a managed domain account for services that extends the standalone managed service account to multiple servers, so it suits server farms and services behind a network load balancer. Mutual authentication protocols require all instances of a service to use the same principal, and a gMSA supplies that single identity without clients needing to know which instance they reach. Windows, not an administrator, manages the password: the Microsoft Key Distribution Service provides keys that change periodically, a domain controller computes the password from the key and gMSA attributes, and member hosts fetch the current and preceding values from a domain controller. This removes the need to synchronize passwords between service instances, and the accounts also support hosts that stay offline for long periods. Failover clusters do not support gMSAs, although services running on a cluster can use one if they are Windows services, app pools or scheduled tasks. Requirements include 64-bit PowerShell tooling, Windows Server 2012 or later, and Kerberos-supported encryption; Microsoft recommends configuring AES for managed service accounts.

group-naming-policy.title: Enforce a naming policy for Microsoft 365 groups (Microsoft Entra)
group-naming-policy.notes: A group naming policy enforces consistent names for Microsoft 365 groups that users create or edit, and can block specific words in names and aliases. It has two parts. The prefix-suffix policy follows the pattern prefix, group name, suffix; fixed strings and user attributes such as department, company, office, state, country or title can be used, and the combined name must fit in 63 characters. Custom blocked words are a comma-separated list of up to 5,000 phrases that are matched exactly, not as substrings, and are not case sensitive. The policy applies across workloads such as Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Planner, to both name and alias. Existing groups are not renamed when the policy is set; it is enforced when an owner edits the group. Global Administrators and User Administrators are exempt. Some clients, including Outlook desktop and mobile and the Microsoft 365 admin center, do not preview the enforced name, and School Data Sync and the Classroom app do not apply it automatically. Configuration is possible in the Entra admin center or with Microsoft Graph PowerShell, and using it requires owning Entra ID P1 licensing for group members.

headless-commerce.title: Headless commerce (Wikipedia)
headless-commerce.notes: Headless commerce is an e-commerce architecture that separates the front end, the head, from the back-end commerce functions, so the presentation layer can be redesigned or replaced without disturbing the back end, much as a headless CMS separates content from presentation. The term was coined in 2013 by Dirk Hoerig, co-founder of Commercetools, and the approach is often traced to a Forrester report that urged loosely coupled front and back ends. The back end handles data and business functionality and exposes it through APIs, mainly REST, so one back end can feed many front ends such as websites, apps, browsers and IoT devices. In traditional monolithic commerce the two are coupled. Claimed benefits are a single place to change data, independent deployment of front ends, flexibility beyond fixed templates, lower operational risk, faster innovation, tailored designs per channel and a consistent omnichannel experience with products and orders managed once. Headless storefronts can use server-side rendering or static generation for fast loads and better SEO. Drawbacks include more development effort, no ready-made templates, the need to build or buy a front end and limited suitability for small businesses.

high-context-communication.title: High-context and low-context cultures (Wikipedia)
high-context-communication.notes: High-context and low-context describe a continuum of how explicit messages are in a culture and how much meaning depends on surrounding context, a framework introduced by anthropologist Edward T. Hall in his 1959 book The Silent Language. In high-context communication much of the meaning is carried by context, relationships, gestures, tone and timing, so messages are often indirect and listeners read small cues; such cultures tend to be relational and collectivist and to value harmony and tradition. Low-context communication places meaning in explicit, direct and detailed words because people cannot assume shared background; these cultures tend to be more individualistic. Hall classed Japanese, Arab and Southern European peoples as high-context and Germans, Scandinavians, Americans and other Northern Europeans as low-context. The page stresses that this is a spectrum, not a binary, and that one country can show both kinds of situation. It also records studies on conflict styles and manager behaviour, a link to Bernstein's restricted and elaborated codes, and a 2008 meta-analysis by Peter Cardon criticizing the model as unsubstantiated and underdeveloped.

honeytoken-accounts.title: Defender for Identity entity tags: honeytoken (Microsoft Learn)
honeytoken-accounts.notes: In Microsoft Defender for Identity, a honeytoken is a decoy entity that you tag so that its use can be detected. These accounts are usually dormant and exist to set traps for malicious actors; since no legitimate user needs them, any activity is suspicious, and the page states that any sign-in from a honeytoken account triggers an alert. The tag supports both users and devices. Tagging is done in Microsoft Defender XDR: open Settings, then Identities, choose the Honeytoken tag, select Tag users or Tag devices, pick the entities from the list and add the selection. Prerequisites are a deployed Defender for Identity environment, access to Microsoft Defender and membership in an appropriate role group. The page does not explain how to create the decoy account itself in Active Directory or Entra ID, nor which alert name or detection timing applies, so those details come from the separate alert documentation.

hub-and-spoke-governance.title: Hub and spoke GRC: central governance with local autonomy (6clicks)
hub-and-spoke-governance.notes: Hub and spoke is a governance architecture that separates standards, set centrally, from day-to-day execution, carried out locally. The central hub defines controls, policies, frameworks and reporting standards that every entity works against. The spokes are local entities that operate independently, running control tests, collecting evidence, handling their own regulatory context and reporting against the hub's requirements; their reporting rolls up so the hub sees a consolidated compliance picture. The article positions the model as a middle path between a fully centralized team that local units disengage from and a fully decentralized setup that produces inconsistent reporting that is hard to consolidate. It says the pattern mirrors how large government departments, defence contractors and multi-subsidiary regulated organizations work. In the vendor's own implementation, hub content such as policies and control libraries is inherited by spokes, which may extend but not override it, dashboards aggregate status across spokes, and suppliers can be included as spokes for vendor risk management. This is vendor material, so benefit claims are the vendor's own.

hyperconverged-infrastructure.title: Hyper-converged infrastructure (Wikipedia)
hyperconverged-infrastructure.notes: Hyper-converged infrastructure is software-defined IT infrastructure that virtualizes the elements of conventional hardware-defined systems, typically on commodity off-the-shelf servers. At minimum it combines three virtualized layers: compute through a hypervisor, storage through software-defined storage and networking through software-defined networking. Systems usually consist of servers with direct-attached storage, and storage-area-network functions are implemented in software at or through the hypervisor instead of in separate physical hardware, which is the main difference from converged infrastructure. Because these functions run in the hypervisor, resources can be managed in a federated way across all instances, similar systems can be pooled and all data-center resources are managed from one administrative platform. Consolidating functions at the hypervisor level was promoted as a way to cut inefficiencies and total cost of ownership, since organizations may no longer need separate compute and storage systems, and it is likely to simplify management and raise utilization where it applies. The page notes it was still too early to show that HCI can replace storage arrays in every market segment, and some of its claims are flagged as needing clarification or sources.

immutable-backup.title: Immutable vaults for Azure Backup (Microsoft Learn)
immutable-backup.notes: An immutable vault is an Azure Backup vault setting that blocks operations which could cause recovery points to be lost, protecting backups from malicious actors who try to delete them or disable protection. With immutability on, three actions are refused: stopping protection with deletion of data before recovery points expire, changing a backup policy to reduce retention, and replacing an item's policy with one that has shorter retention; increasing retention or changing the schedule stays allowed. The vault can be in one of three states: disabled, enabled (blocking risky operations but reversible) or enabled and locked, which is irreversible and uses WORM storage. Microsoft recommends locking once the impact is understood so attackers cannot switch it off. Immutability can follow the backup policy by default, or be set for a fixed number of days applied to all recovery points. It covers Recovery Services vaults and Backup vaults and all workloads Azure Backup protects, though operational backups of blobs, files and disks are excluded. The Microsoft.RecoveryServices resource provider must be registered in the subscription.

immutable-storage.title: Immutable storage for Azure Blob Storage (Microsoft Learn)
immutable-storage.notes: Immutable storage keeps business-critical blob data in a write once, read many state so that it cannot be modified or deleted for a user-specified interval, even by users with account administrative privileges. Two policy types exist and can be combined: time-based retention, where objects can be created and read but not changed or deleted until the interval ends (1 day to 146,000 days), and legal holds, which protect data until the hold is explicitly cleared and carry user-defined tags such as a case ID. Time-based policies can be unlocked, for testing and changeable, or locked, for compliance, which cannot be shortened or removed; Microsoft recommends locking within about 24 hours. WORM can be applied at container level or, with versioning enabled, at account, container or version level. It is designed to help meet SEC 17a-4(f), CFTC and FINRA rules, and Cohasset Associates validated it. No extra capacity charge applies. Limits include incompatibility with point-in-time restore, NFS 3.0 and SFTP accounts, and failure of workloads that append to existing blobs unless protected append writes are allowed.

import-mode.title: Storage mode in Power BI Desktop (Microsoft Learn)
import-mode.notes: Import is one of the Power BI storage modes, alongside DirectQuery and Dual, and it determines whether data is cached in memory for reports or queried from the source when visuals load. In Import mode a snapshot of the source data is stored in native in-memory storage, so visuals load quickly; it is available for almost all data sources through Get data and Power Query. The trade-off is freshness: data is only as current as the last refresh, so the semantic model or table must be refreshed to see newer data. DirectQuery works the other way, translating DAX queries to the source's native language at view time, giving results closer to real time but potentially slower queries and with limits on transformations and DAX in calculated columns. Dual tables can act as either Import or DirectQuery and mainly resolve limited relationships between the two, for example by caching dimension tables so slicers load quickly while a large fact table stays in DirectQuery. A DirectQuery table can later be changed to Import or Dual but not back to DirectQuery, with web modeling as an exception.

independent-software-vendor.title: Independent software vendor (Wikipedia)
independent-software-vendor.notes: An independent software vendor, also called a software publisher, is an organization that makes and sells software rather than hardware, for mass or niche markets. The page separates ISV software from in-house software, built by the user organization, and from custom software, designed or adapted for one specific third party: ISV products are sold to many customers while the vendor keeps ownership. Examples of uses include software for real estate brokers, healthcare scheduling, barcode scanning, retail, energy exploration and fleet management. ISV products run on one or more hardware or operating system platforms, and platform companies such as Microsoft, AWS, Cisco, IBM, Red Hat, Oracle, Apple, SAP and Salesforce support them, often through business partner programs from which both sides gain new opportunities. ISVs are described as one of the primary groups in the IT industry and often act as channels that spread new technologies and solutions. A company can be both a platform provider and an ISV, as Microsoft, Red Hat, Canonical, Adobe and Oracle are cited as examples.

indicators-of-compromise.title: Indicator of compromise (Wikipedia)
indicators-of-compromise.notes: An indicator of compromise is a technical artifact or observable event on a network or system that suggests an attack is coming or underway, or that a compromise has already occurred. Examples are virus signatures, suspicious IP addresses, file hashes of malware, malicious URLs or domains tied to botnet command servers, and the subject line of a malicious email. Indicators are often ranked in the Pyramid of Pain by how hard they are for an attacker to change: file hashes are exact but trivially defeated by recompiling, IPs and domains sit higher, and tactics, techniques and procedures are costly to change. Defenses such as firewalls, IDS and IPS, antivirus, EDR and SIEM platforms consume them, and defenders also check new indicators against historical logs to find past intrusions. Formats and protocols for sharing include STIX, TAXII, OpenIOC, MISP and IODEF, with the Traffic Light Protocol limiting redistribution. RFC 9424 describes a lifecycle of discovery, assessment, sharing, deployment and retirement, and stresses that every indicator trades false positives against missed attacks and that specific indicators are fragile.

inforcer.title: Microsoft 365 multi-tenant management (Inforcer)
inforcer.notes: Inforcer is a multi-tenant management platform for Microsoft 365 built for managed service providers, which the company says is used by more than 1,000 MSPs. Its core idea is to define a baseline once and deploy it across many customer tenants or tenant groups, detect tenants that drift from the standard and push fixes from one dashboard. Baselines can be custom or aligned to frameworks such as CIS, Essential 8, Cyber Essentials and NIS2. The platform monitors changes to policies, settings and assignments, raises alerts for items such as certificate expiry or Secure Score drops, and can create tickets in PSA tools like Autotask, ConnectWise and Halo or notify through Teams, Slack or webhooks. It covers Intune, Defender, Entra ID, Exchange Online Protection, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams and Purview, and tenants can be onboarded from Partner Center. Product lines named are 365 Manager and inforcer TDR for threat detection and response. The page makes vendor claims about onboarding time savings, and lists regional portals for the UK, US, EU and ANZ.

information-asymmetry.title: Information asymmetry (Wikipedia)
information-asymmetry.notes: Information asymmetry exists when one party in a transaction has more or better information than the other, shifting bargaining power and potentially making transactions inefficient or even causing market failure. It is a core concept in contract theory, mechanism design and economics. The classic problems are adverse selection, where the uninformed side cannot tell good from bad, as in Akerlof's 1970 used-car lemons market, and moral hazard, where a party takes more risk after a deal because it does not bear the full consequences. Responses include signalling, where an informed party shows its type credibly, as Spence described with education, and screening, where the uninformed party offers choices that make the other reveal private information, developed by Stiglitz. Other examples are health insurance death spirals, credence goods whose quality cannot be verified even after use, and principal-agent problems. Countermeasures listed include warranties, brand names, lemon laws, mandatory disclosure, incentive alignment, third-party checks and certification. Akerlof, Spence and Stiglitz shared the 2001 Nobel Prize for work on markets with asymmetric information.

infrastructure-chaining.title: Using infrastructure analysis to get ahead of attacks in cyber defense, part 2 (DomainTools)
infrastructure-chaining.notes: This DomainTools article covers infrastructure pivoting, the technique also called infrastructure chaining. It begins with a single indicator, usually a suspicious domain such as a newly registered one that spoofs an organization or partner, and studies the registration and hosting data around it to find other infrastructure that seems to be preparing for later attack stages. The page treats such a hit as an early-stage signal, comparable to resource development or initial access in ATT&CK. A pivoting tool maps related infrastructure through shared linking data points. Attributes named include the registrar, SSL certificate metadata such as organization names and self-signed certificates, name servers, IP addresses with ranges, ASNs and hosting providers, plus naming schemes, creation dates within narrow ranges and MX or SPF records. Each attribute can look unremarkable alone, but combining them lets analysts triangulate a set of common infrastructure and reveal a larger campaign that may be active or dormant. Findings can feed detection, blocking, email quarantine and packet inspection rules. The article is vendor-authored and uses the term pivoting rather than chaining.

integration-service-environment.title: Act now: Azure app platform and integration services retiring on 31 August 2024 (Microsoft Tech Community)
integration-service-environment.notes: This Microsoft Tech Community announcement states that the Azure Logic Apps Integration Service Environment is retired on 31 August 2024, and names Logic Apps Standard as the migration target. The post gives reasons for choosing Standard: better compute and network isolation, high availability with compute elasticity and an improved development experience. It points customers to a migration guide, to Microsoft's guidance for exporting ISE workflows to a Standard logic app, and to an episode of the FastTrack for Azure Learn Live series that covers the ISE to Standard move. Customers who run into roadblocks are told to contact their Microsoft account team or partner, or to use FastTrack for Azure. The same article also covers the retirement of App Service Environment versions 1 and 2 and API Management stv1, which are separate from ISE. The page is a retirement notice and does not describe in detail how ISE worked.

intelligent-document-processing.title: What is Azure Document Intelligence? (Microsoft Learn)
intelligent-document-processing.notes: Azure Document Intelligence is a cloud service for building intelligent document processing solutions. It uses machine-learning-based OCR and extraction to turn forms and documents, such as invoices, receipts, IDs and tax forms, into structured data that applications and workflows can use, so that businesses can handle large volumes of varied documents faster, automate processes and enrich document search. Model families include general analysis models (Read for printed and handwritten text, Layout for text, tables and structure), many prebuilt models that need no training (invoices, receipts, bank statements, US tax forms, mortgage forms, ID documents and others), and custom models trained on labeled data, with neural, template and composed extraction types plus custom classification that identifies document types before extraction. Extracted values come back as typed fields such as string, number, date, currency and address. Optional add-ons include high-resolution extraction, formulas, fonts, barcodes, query fields and searchable PDF output. The page contrasts its deterministic extraction for structured documents with LLM-powered analyzers in Azure Content Understanding, and lists version support, with v4.0 current.

internal-carbon-fee.title: Microsoft's carbon fee, 3 years later (Microsoft Green Blog)
internal-carbon-fee.notes: In this 2015 Microsoft blog post, the carbon fee is described as an internal charge linked to the company's July 2012 commitment to carbon neutrality, which holds business groups financially responsible for the cost of reducing and offsetting their carbon emissions. Groups pay based on their emissions, and the post does not state a price per ton. The fee funds purchases of more than 10 billion kWh of green power, carbon offset projects in emerging nations said to affect over 3.2 million people, more than 60 projects in 23 countries that reduce Microsoft's footprint, renewable energy deals such as the Keechi Wind Project in Texas, and clean energy research including fuel cell pilots and a biogas-powered small datacenter in Wyoming. Microsoft reported emissions cuts of 7.5 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent and savings above 10 million dollars per year, and said the US EPA ranked it the second-largest US green power purchaser. The company says the fee makes carbon costs visible and pushes groups to seek further reductions. The figures are the company's own 2015 reporting, and a whitepaper was released alongside the post.

intune-update-rings.title: Manage Windows update rings in Microsoft Intune (Microsoft Learn)
intune-update-rings.notes: Windows update rings are Intune policies that control how and when Windows updates install by configuring client-side Windows Update behavior: deferral periods, restart settings, deadlines, active hours and user notifications. Organizations often use several rings to stage deployments, for example test, pilot and production, by assigning different settings to different device groups, and rings can be combined with feature, quality and driver update policies. Supported editions include Pro, Pro Education, Enterprise, Education, IoT Enterprise and Team; LTSC editions get quality updates only, so feature update controls do not apply. Prerequisites are Intune Plan 1, internet access to Intune, Windows Update and Autopatch endpoints, and the Microsoft Account Sign-In Assistant service running. A ring is created in the admin center under Windows updates, then assigned; Microsoft advises assigning to device groups rather than user groups so the policy applies without a sign-in. Reports show check-in status, assignment status and per-setting status. Deleting a ring stops enforcement but does not undo settings already on devices. Devices managed by Windows Autopatch may have rings created for them, so custom rings should not normally be assigned there.

jamf-pro.title: Integrate Jamf Pro with Intune for compliance (Microsoft Learn)
jamf-pro.notes: This Microsoft Learn page explains how Jamf Pro, a management tool for Macs, can be integrated with Microsoft Intune so that Jamf-managed macOS devices must meet Intune compliance requirements before they reach organizational resources. Jamf Pro syncs macOS inventory to Intune through Microsoft Entra ID, Intune's compliance engine evaluates it, and the result is combined with the user's Entra identity to enforce Conditional Access just as for devices managed directly by Intune. Microsoft recommends the Jamf Cloud Connector, while the article covers the manual method: register an app in Entra with specific API permissions, enable the Compliance Connector for Jamf in Intune under partner device management, configure the integration in Jamf Pro, set enrollment group assignments and deploy the Company Portal app. Prerequisites include Jamf Pro 10.1.0 or later, Intune and Entra ID P1 licensing and macOS 10.12 or later. A deprecation notice says Jamf's macOS Conditional Access feature relied on a platform no longer supported from January 31, 2025, so customers should move to the Device Compliance integration. Disconnecting removes devices from Intune after about three months.

jump-box.title: Jump server (Wikipedia)
jump-box.notes: A jump server, also called a jump host or jump box, is a hardened and monitored system on a network that administrators use to reach and manage devices in a separate security zone, sitting between two dissimilar zones to give controlled access, commonly for managing hosts in a DMZ from trusted internal networks. The idea emerged in the 1990s with co-location facilities, was often paired with a SOCKS proxy, and became the standard approach once SSH tunneling spread. An administrator logs into the jump server first and then reaches the target; typical builds are a hardened Unix-like machine with SSH and a local firewall, or a Windows server running Remote Desktop Services. Benefits include a single audit point, central account management and logging of all access. The page stresses that a jump server is itself a risk and recommends proper network segmentation, multi-factor authentication, regular patching, access control lists, blocking its outbound internet access, limiting which programs may run and detailed logging with alerts. When richer control of client environments is needed, a VPN may be more suitable.

keda.title: KEDA concepts (keda.sh documentation)
keda.notes: KEDA, created by Microsoft and Red Hat, is a lightweight tool that helps Kubernetes scale applications based on real-world events. It sits alongside the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler instead of replacing it, extending scaling beyond CPU and memory, and you choose which workloads use it. It watches external event sources such as message queues, databases and APIs and adjusts pod counts to match demand. The keda-operator handles scaling between zero and one replica, while the metrics server exposes external metrics so the autoscaler can manage one to N replicas. Admission webhooks catch configuration errors such as two ScaledObjects targeting the same Deployment. Key resources are ScaledObject, which links a Deployment or StatefulSet to an event source, ScaledJob, which creates Kubernetes Jobs per event such as one per queue message, and TriggerAuthentication for credentials. Scalers connect KEDA to sources including Kafka, RabbitMQ, Prometheus, AWS SQS, Redis and PostgreSQL, and custom scalers can be built. CPU and memory triggers cannot scale to zero, because without running pods there is no metric data to trigger scale-up.

key-performance-indicator.title: Performance indicator (Wikipedia)
key-performance-indicator.notes: A key performance indicator is a measurement used to judge how well an organization, project, process or activity is meeting defined objectives, helping focus improvement and support evidence-based decisions. Indicators can be grouped by perspective, as in the balanced scorecard's financial, customer, internal process and learning views; by time orientation, as lagging (past results), leading (predictive) and input (resources); by data type, quantitative or qualitative; and by level. Choosing them is a managerial decision about what success means; frameworks include SMART and FABRIC, and good indicators are simple, precise, balanced, hard to manipulate and backed by verifiable data. The page lists examples across finance, customers, manufacturing, services, supply chain and HR, and describes government use for accountability. It also records limits: oversimplification, gaming and perverse incentives such as Vietnam body counts or counting lines of code, tunnel vision, poor data, monitoring burden and blindness to context. Suggested mitigations include co-designing indicators with frontline staff, reviewing them regularly, mixing quantitative and qualitative data and auditing for gaming.

krbtgt-account.title: Resetting the krbtgt password (Microsoft Learn)
krbtgt-account.notes: This Learn article covers resetting the built-in krbtgt account of an Active Directory domain as part of forest recovery. The reset applies to writable domain controllers, not read-only ones, and each read-only DC has its own account named krbtgt followed by an underscore and a number, which should not be deleted if you plan to recover that RODC. The password must be reset twice because the account's password history keeps the two most recent values; resetting twice pushes all old passwords out of history, so no domain controller can replicate using an old one. At least 10 hours must pass between the two resets, matching the default maximum lifetime of user and service tickets, and the wait should be longer if those lifetimes were raised. To reset, open Active Directory Users and Computers, enable Advanced Features, open the Users container, right-click krbtgt and choose Reset Password; the value typed does not matter because the system generates a strong password. A custom password filter such as passfilt.dll can make the reset fail. The procedure applies to Windows Server 2016 through 2025.

kv-cache.title: KV cache strategies (Hugging Face Transformers documentation)
kv-cache.notes: In autoregressive transformer models each new token is predicted from all previous ones, and attention needs key and value vectors for every earlier position. A KV cache stores these so they can be reused instead of recomputed at every step, cutting computation and improving response time. The prompt is processed once in a prefill step, and then each decoding step computes only the new token's key and value, appends them to the cache and attends over the stored history. The page warns that the cache can take a significant share of memory and become a bottleneck for long-context generation. The default dynamic cache grows with each token, although sliding-window or chunked-attention layers stop growing at the window size, while a static cache pre-allocates a fixed maximum, enabling compilation at the cost of wasted slots. Memory can be reduced by offloading all but the current layer's cache to the CPU, which may cost throughput, or by quantizing the cache to lower precision, which can hurt latency on short contexts. Further features include rolling back tokens, reusing a cached prefix and caches for encoder-decoder models; state-space models like Mamba need their own cache types.

ldap.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (Wikipedia)
ldap.notes: LDAP is an application protocol for accessing and maintaining directory information services over IP networks, following the X.500 data and service models in a lighter form that runs over TCP/IP, which is why it was nicknamed X.500 Lite. A common use is a central store of usernames and passwords that many applications check. It was created around 1993 by Tim Howes, Steve Kille, Colin Robbins and Wengyik Yeong; LDAPv3 work began in 1996 to 1997 and LDAPv2 was retired in 2003, and it underpins Microsoft Active Directory. A client connects to a server and every session starts anonymous until a Bind operation authenticates it. Operations include Search, Compare, Add, Delete, Modify, Modify DN and StartTLS. Data is organized as entries made of attributes, each entry identified by a distinguished name much like a file path, and a schema defines the permitted object classes and attributes. Port 389 is standard, with StartTLS upgrading to encryption, and 636 is used for LDAPS. Simple bind sends credentials in plaintext, so TLS should be required, and unsanitized input can cause LDAP injection.

license-plate.title: License plate build in Dynamics 365 warehouse management (Microsoft Learn)
license-plate.notes: In Dynamics 365 warehouse management, a license plate is a unique identifier assigned to a group of items. The page does not use the word container, but plates act like one: items sharing a plate can be tracked and moved as a single unit instead of individually, which reduces the effort of managing inventory. License plates can be nested, with several child plates assigned to one parent, forming a tree whose root is the parent and whose leaves are the plates holding on-hand inventory. The License plate build menu item in the Warehouse Management mobile app lets a user choose a parent and assign children, but only if the parent holds no on-hand inventory and the plates with inventory are the leaves. Moving the parent then moves all nested inventory in one action, which streamlines work. Microsoft says parent plates should never hold on-hand inventory, and that doing so is not fully supported. Setup involves creating an indirect-mode mobile menu item without process guide and adding it to the mobile device menu. Parent plates also matter for advance ship notices.

linq.title: Language Integrated Query (LINQ) in C# (Microsoft Learn)
linq.notes: Language Integrated Query is a set of technologies that builds query capabilities directly into C#. Before it, queries were plain strings without compile-time type checking or IntelliSense, and each data source had its own language, such as SQL or XPath. With LINQ a query is a first-class language construct, and the same declarative query expressions, with from, where and select clauses for filtering, ordering and grouping, work across any LINQ-enabled data source, so one query can read a SQL database and produce XML. Variables in a query are strongly typed, and execution is deferred until the query is iterated, for example in a foreach loop. The compiler turns query expressions into standard query operator method calls, and anything written in query syntax can also be written in method syntax with no semantic or performance difference; operations such as Count and Max exist only as methods. Queries over IEnumerable of T compile to delegates (LINQ to Objects), while IQueryable queries compile to expression trees, which a provider such as Entity Framework Core can translate into SQL. Remote sources should implement IQueryable.

liquid.title: Liquid reference (Shopify developer documentation)
liquid.notes: Liquid is a template language created by Shopify and available as an open-source project on GitHub, used by many software projects and companies. A template holds static content and inserts dynamic information depending on where it is rendered, so one product template can show the image, title and price of whichever product is viewed. Liquid outputs objects and their properties, written in double curly braces with dot notation, and modifies output with tags and filters. Tags are logic instructions in curly-brace-percent delimiters that are not rendered, for example an if tag, a for loop with an optional limit, or the liquid tag that nests several tags in one set of delimiters. Filters change the output of variables and are applied with the pipe character, chained from left to right, and many take parameters. Objects represent store resources such as products and collections, standard content and interactive elements like pagination and search, and custom variables can be created with tags such as assign and capture. Shopify extends open-source Liquid with its own tags, filters and objects, and several other Shopify features use modified versions.

llmlingua.title: LLMLingua series (Microsoft Research)
llmlingua.notes: The LLMLingua series from Microsoft Research is a set of prompt compression methods that shorten long prompts so large language models process them faster, more cheaply and more effectively. Prompts built with chain-of-thought, in-context learning or retrieval can reach tens of thousands of tokens, causing slower responses, exceeded context windows, higher cost and the lost-in-the-middle problem. The original LLMLingua uses perplexity from a small language model to find and drop non-essential tokens, reported to reach up to 20 times compression with little performance loss, and GPT-4 can recover key information from a compressed prompt. LongLLMLingua targets long contexts with query-aware compression and reordering, reported to improve performance by 17.1 percent at 4 times compression. LLMLingua-2 treats compression as token classification with a BERT-level encoder trained by distillation from GPT-4, is task-agnostic, handles out-of-domain data better and is reported to be 3 to 6 times faster than LLMLingua. The methods have been integrated into LangChain and LlamaIndex, and the page notes the project is for research demonstration purposes.

llmops.title: GenAIOps (LLMOps) maturity model (Microsoft Learn)
llmops.notes: Microsoft Learn defines generative AI operations, also called LLMOps, as the operational practices and strategies for managing large language models in production, and offers a four-level maturity model scored by an assessment questionnaire. Level 1, Initial, covers exploring LLM APIs, basic prompt design and simple performance metrics. Level 2, Defined, adds systematic development and deployment, possibly with CI/CD, more advanced evaluation such as groundedness, relevance and similarity, and a focus on content safety. Level 3, Managed, brings proactive monitoring with predictive analytics, fine-tuning and advanced version control with rollback. Level 4, Optimized, stresses operational excellence, alignment with business goals, keeping up with LLM advances and sharing knowledge. Key practices named across the levels are evaluation, monitoring, deployment, versioning, content safety and fine-tuning. The page warns that Prompt flow in Foundry and Azure Machine Learning is scheduled for retirement on April 20, 2027, and recommends migrating to Microsoft Agent Framework. It also links learning paths and a workshop for each level.

location-directive.title: Work with location directives (Microsoft Learn)
location-directive.notes: Location directives are user-defined rules in Dynamics 365 warehouse management that decide where inventory is picked from and where it is put, for example which locations feed a sales order and where picked items go. Each directive is created for a work order type and applies only to the Warehouse management module. It consists of a header (sequence number, name, work type of put or pick, scope, warehouse selection), lines that set quantity conditions, and actions that find the best location using queries and predefined strategies such as consolidate, empty location with no incoming work, FEFO batch reservation, license plate guided and location aging FIFO or LIFO. The system tries directives in ascending sequence order, or by directive code when one is tied to a step of a work template, evaluates lines by quantity range and runs actions in sequence. If nothing is found, behavior depends on the location directive failures setup: work may be created without locations or fail. Uses include put-away, picking and staging, raw material handling and replenishment, and directives can be tested with acceptance tests.

logic-apps-stateful-workflows.title: Stateful and stateless workflows in Standard logic apps (Microsoft Learn)
logic-apps-stateful-workflows.notes: In Azure Logic Apps Standard you pick the workflow type at creation, and changing it later causes runtime errors. Stateful workflows save all operation inputs, outputs and states to external storage, so run history can be reviewed after each run and interrupted runs can be reconstructed and rerun after an outage. They can run longer, with the default maximum duration editable in host configuration, support managed connector triggers and the Recurrence trigger, handle large messages with chunking and run asynchronously, where an HTTP 202 response with a location header lets callers poll for status. Stateless workflows keep data in memory only, store no run history by default, are not restored after outages, usually finish within five minutes and are best for content of about 64 KB or less. They allow only push-style triggers such as Request, Event Hubs or Service Bus, no chunking, and synchronous execution only, but offer the quickest responses, higher throughput and lower cost. The page also tabulates how parent and child workflows of each type behave.

lotus-1-2-3.title: Lotus 1-2-3 (Wikipedia)
lotus-1-2-3.notes: Lotus 1-2-3 was a spreadsheet program from Lotus Development Corporation, later part of IBM, released on 26 January 1983 for DOS-based PCs. Its name reflects three integrated functions: spreadsheet calculation, charting and basic database operations such as sorting. Early releases were written mainly in x86 assembly, credited for speed, and later releases were converted to C. It became the killer application for the IBM PC, outselling VisiCalc; it sold 175,000 copies in its first year, 3.5 million by 1988, and a 1990 survey found 62 percent of spreadsheet users used it. Features included keyboard menus, macros, add-ins from version 2.0 and 3D spreadsheets from Release 3. The page records legal disputes, including Lotus v. Borland, which ended in a 4-4 Supreme Court split in 1996. Release 3 was delayed by more than a year, and Microsoft Excel, first on the Macintosh in 1985 and Windows in 1987, gained ground as Windows spread, while a Windows rewrite failed. IBM bought Lotus in 1995, announced the brand's withdrawal in 2013 and ended support on 30 September 2014. It treated 1900 as a leap year, an error Excel copied for compatibility.

magma.title: Magma: A Foundation Model for Multimodal AI Agents (arXiv)
magma.notes: Magma is a foundation model from Microsoft Research and collaborating universities for multimodal AI agents that act in both digital interfaces and physical robot settings. It extends vision-language models, keeping their understanding ability while adding planning and action in visual-spatial environments. Pretraining uses roughly 39 million samples drawn from UI screenshots, robot trajectories from Open X-Embodiment, instructional videos and image-text understanding data. Two techniques unify the data: Set-of-Mark, which numbers actionable regions so the model selects marks rather than raw pixel coordinates, and Trace-of-Mark, which tracks points across future frames to teach motion. All actions are converted to text tokens. The model combines a ConvNeXt-XXLarge vision encoder with a LLaMA-3-8B language model. Reported results include beating GPT-4V with OmniParser zero-shot on UI benchmarks such as ScreenSpot, outperforming OpenVLA on robot tasks in SimplerEnv, and strong spatial reasoning. The authors note it is meant for controlled web and Android simulators and specific robot setups, recommend human oversight for UI actions and mention possible biases and misuse through fine-tuning.

mainframe-computer.title: Mainframe computer (Wikipedia)
mainframe-computer.notes: A mainframe is a computer used mainly by large organizations for critical work such as bulk data processing, enterprise resource planning and large-scale transaction processing, sitting above minicomputers and workstations but below supercomputers in scale and often serving as a server. The name comes from the large cabinet, the main frame, that held the CPU and memory of early machines. Typical traits are very high reliability and availability through redundant engineering, strong security, separate I/O subsystems, strict backward compatibility, virtualization with multiple operating system instances such as IBM Z logical partitions, hot-swappable components and execution integrity checks that run instructions twice. Early mainframes in the 1950s ran batch jobs from punched cards and tape; timesharing with terminals followed, IBM's System/360 was a 1960s milestone, and desktop sales first exceeded mainframe sales in 1984. Demand recovered in the late 1990s with e-business and Linux on mainframes, and IBM introduced 64-bit z/Architecture in 2000, later reaching the z16 in 2022 with an on-chip AI accelerator. Mainframes focus on transactions and I/O, while supercomputers focus on floating-point science.

market-development-funds.title: FY25 Microsoft Partner Incentives Co-op Guidebook
market-development-funds.notes: The Microsoft Partner Incentives Co-op Guidebook (FY25 edition, hosted by a distributor) explains Microsoft's cooperative marketing funds. Co-op reimburses partners for marketing and skilling activities that build awareness of Microsoft products, and it is described as a reward partners reinvest in their Microsoft business. Partners in eligible incentive programs receive part of their payout as a monthly rebate and part as Co-op, accrued over six-month periods of the fiscal calendar, and they must reach a minimum earning threshold, for example 1,500 USD for Surface resellers and 10,000 USD for CSP partners, or lose access to the accrued amount. Spending means completing an approved activity, collecting proof of execution and filing a claim in Partner Center. Eligible categories are demand generation, market development and partner skilling. Claim deadlines fall in February for the July to December half and in August for January to June; unclaimed funds are forfeited with no rollover. Partners keep proof for 24 months, and ineligible costs include staff travel in most cases and operating expenses.

material-requirements-planning.title: Material requirements planning (Wikipedia)
material-requirements-planning.notes: Material requirements planning is a system for production planning, scheduling and inventory control in manufacturing, mostly software-based though it can be done by hand. It aims to do three things at once: have raw materials available for production and finished goods ready for delivery, keep material and product stock as low as possible, and plan manufacturing, delivery schedules and purchasing together. The page does not explain the calculation or inputs. Its history section says manufacturers earlier used reorder point, reorder quantity and economic order quantity methods, that Rolls-Royce and General Electric computerized the idea in the early 1950s without commercializing it, and that Joseph Orlicky developed MRP in 1964, with Black and Decker as first adopter. Orlicky published a book in 1975, when about 700 companies used it, rising to roughly 8,000 by 1981. Oliver Wight developed manufacturing resource planning, MRP II, in 1983, adding master scheduling, rough-cut capacity planning, capacity requirements planning and sales and operations planning. A 1986 article reported an average 200 percent return on investment for full MRP II users.

material-ui.title: Material UI: Overview (MUI)
material-ui.notes: Material UI is an open-source React component library that implements Google's Material Design. It offers a broad set of prebuilt components that can be used in production as they are, plus customization options for building a custom design system on top of them. The documentation says it supports Material Design 2, follows the specification closely and departs from it where needed to offer alternative options, with later design updates tracked in a GitHub issue. Besides components it provides theming and customization features, templates in the MUI store showing how far customization can go, design kits including a Figma resource, and learning material such as installation guides, example projects and a list of free templates. The project dates back to 2014, has more than 2,500 open-source contributors and describes itself as having the largest UI community in the React ecosystem, with community help available on Stack Overflow. The page shows version 9.5.0 and a banner announcing that Material UI and MUI X version 9 are out.

mathematical-optimization.title: Mathematical optimization (Wikipedia)
mathematical-optimization.notes: Mathematical optimization, also called mathematical programming, is the selection of a best element, by some criterion, from a set of available alternatives. The general task is to maximize or minimize a real-valued objective function by systematically choosing inputs from an allowed set; since maximizing a function equals minimizing its negative, problems are usually stated as minimization. The objective goes by names such as cost, loss, utility or fitness, and the allowed set, often defined by equality or inequality constraints, is the search space whose members are feasible solutions. Constraints can change the answer compared with the unconstrained optimum. The field divides into discrete and continuous optimization and includes convex programming, with linear, second-order cone and semidefinite programming as special cases, plus integer, quadratic, nonlinear, stochastic and robust optimization, combinatorial problems and multi-objective optimization. Local minima are only best nearby, whereas a global minimum is best overall; in convex problems any local minimum is global. Methods include finite algorithms such as simplex, iterative methods such as gradient descent and Newton's method, and heuristics such as genetic algorithms that give no optimality guarantee.

max-cut.title: Maximum cut (Wikipedia)
max-cut.notes: A maximum cut of a graph is a partition of its vertices into two sets so that the number of edges between the sets is at least as large as for any other partition; equivalently it is a bipartite subgraph with as many edges as possible. In the weighted version each edge has a weight and the total weight across the cut is maximized. The decision version is NP-complete, with the weighted case among Karp's 21 NP-complete problems, and the optimization version is NP-hard, while the opposite problem, minimum cut, is solvable efficiently. Max-cut can be solved in polynomial time on planar graphs, and it is fixed-parameter tractable in the cut size. It is APX-hard, so no polynomial-time approximation scheme exists unless P equals NP. A random assignment cuts half the edges in expectation, giving a 0.5-approximation, and local search achieves the same. Goemans and Williamson use semidefinite programming with randomized rounding for the best known ratio, which is optimal under the Unique Games Conjecture. Applications include binary classification, spin glass energy minimization in statistical physics and VLSI circuit layout.

micro-orm.title: Dapper (DapperLib on GitHub)
micro-orm.notes: Dapper is an open-source object mapper for .NET, originally built for and used in production at Stack Overflow, and it is the best-known example of a micro-ORM. It is a lightweight layer over ADO.NET that adds extension methods to database connections so developers run their own SQL and map results onto plain objects. It deliberately covers the common 95 percent of cases and leaves out many features of full ORMs. The core API includes Execute for commands and Query, QuerySingle and variants for typed or dynamic rows. Parameters can be anonymous objects, dictionaries or dynamic parameter bags, lists expand into in clauses, and one command can run against many parameter sets. Further features are multi-mapping, where one row fills several related objects, multiple result sets, stored procedure support and buffered or unbuffered streaming. Dapper has no database-specific code and works with any ADO.NET provider, such as SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle and SQLite. Related packages add Entity Framework handlers, a SQL builder and Dapper.Rainbow, a micro-ORM with CRUD helpers. The page warns that generating many unparameterized SQL strings can cause cache memory issues.
